subject: English
chapter: First Flight (Prose): A Letter to God
text: A Letter to God by G.L. Fuentes. Lencho, a hard-working farmer, depends on rain for his ripe corn crop. A destructive hailstorm ruins his entire harvest, leaving his family fearing hunger. Having deep faith in God, Lencho writes a letter to God asking for 100 pesos to sow again. The postmaster, amused and moved by his faith, collects money from employees and himself, but manages only 70 pesos. When Lencho counts it, he is not surprised (his faith is absolute) but angry that money is short — he assumes the post office employees, whom he calls 'a bunch of crooks', stole the rest. Themes: unquestioning faith versus human doubt, irony, and human goodness/charity.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight (Prose): Nelson Mandela - Long Walk to Freedom
text: This extract from Nelson Mandela's autobiography describes his inauguration as South Africa's first Black president (1994) after the end of apartheid. Mandela honours the freedom fighters who sacrificed for liberty. He reflects that apartheid created a deep wound but also produced people of great courage and character. He defines true freedom as being freedom for all — the oppressor must also be liberated, for a man who takes away another's freedom is himself a prisoner of hatred. He credits his people's courage and speaks of the twin obligations every man has: to his family and to his community/country. Themes: freedom, equality, courage, sacrifice, and the evil of racial discrimination.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight (Prose): Two Stories About Flying
text: Two stories. Part 1 'His First Flight' (Liam O'Flaherty): a young seagull is afraid to fly and stays alone on the ledge while his family flies. Driven by hunger, when his mother brings fish just out of reach, he dives off and discovers he can fly — fear is overcome by necessity and courage. Part 2 'The Black Aeroplane' (Frederick Forsyth): a pilot flying to England in the night sees storm clouds; a mysterious black aeroplane guides him safely through the storm to land. Later he learns no other plane was on the radar — the rescue is unexplained. Themes: overcoming fear, courage, and the mysterious/inexplicable in life.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight (Prose): From the Diary of Anne Frank
text: An extract from the real diary of Anne Frank, a Jewish girl who hid from the Nazis during World War II. Anne treats her diary as a true friend named 'Kitty', pouring out her feelings since she felt no one truly understood her. She humorously describes her family, school life, and her strict maths teacher Mr Keesing, who punishes her talkativeness with essays; her witty essays eventually make him laugh and stop punishing her. The diary reveals her loneliness, intelligence, humour and hope. Themes: loneliness and the need to express oneself, the horror of war and persecution, and the resilient spirit of a young girl.

subject: English
text: Three travel pieces. (1) 'A Baker from Goa' (Lucio Rodrigues): nostalgia for the traditional Goan baker (pader), whose bread is essential to Goan festivals and life. (2) 'Coorg' (Lokesh Abrol): describes the beautiful coffee-growing region of Coorg in Karnataka — its brave Kodava people (of possible Greek/Arab descent), rivers, wildlife, and adventure sports. (3) 'Tea from Assam' (Arup Kumar Datta): Rajvir and Pranjol travel through the vast tea gardens of Assam, the largest tea-growing region; legends about the origin of tea (Chinese and Indian). Themes: the cultural, natural and culinary diversity of India, and appreciation of local traditions.

subject: English
text: Mijbil the Otter by Gavin Maxwell. The author, after losing his dog, decides to keep an otter as a pet and gets one (Mijbil) in Iraq. Mij is playful, affectionate and mischievous — he loves water and plays with a ball, marbles and taps. Transporting him to England by air is challenging; the author packs him in a box, and Mij causes chaos but is finally carried on the lap. In London, Mij becomes a loved companion, and people mistake this unusual pet for various animals. Themes: the bond between humans and animals, the playful nature of pets, and the joy and responsibility of caring for an animal.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight (Prose): Madam Rides the Bus
text: Madam Rides the Bus by Vallikkannan. Valli, an eight-year-old curious girl, longs to ride the town bus she watches daily. She secretly saves money, and one day takes the round-trip journey alone, observing the world with wonder and confidence. She refuses help, acting grown-up ('madam'). On the way she sees a dead cow, which introduces her to the reality of death and dampens her joy. She returns home before anyone notices. Themes: childhood curiosity and desire for independence, the innocence and confidence of a child, and the first awareness of life and death.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight (Prose): The Sermon at Benares
text: The Sermon at Benares by Betty Renshaw retells the story of Gautama Buddha. Kisa Gotami, grief-stricken by the death of her only son, wanders asking for medicine to bring him back. The Buddha asks her to bring a handful of mustard seeds from a house where no one has ever died. She goes from door to door but finds no such house — every family has faced death. She realises death is common to all and inevitable; grief is universal. She gains peace and understanding. Themes: the inevitability and universality of death, the futility of excessive grief, and finding peace through wisdom and acceptance.

subject: English
text: The Proposal by Anton Chekhov is a one-act comedy. Lomov, a nervous, hypochondriac landowner, visits his neighbour Chubukov to propose marriage to his daughter Natalya. Before proposing, Lomov and Natalya quarrel bitterly over the ownership of a piece of land (Oxen Meadows), then over whose dog is better (Squeezer vs Guess). The arguments become absurd and heated, with Chubukov joining in. Amidst the chaos, Chubukov hurriedly joins their hands and blesses the marriage even as they continue to argue. Themes: satire on marriage as a practical/property arrangement, the quarrelsome nature of people, and humour arising from trivial disputes.

subject: English
text: Dust of Snow by Robert Frost is a short poem about how a small moment in nature can change one's mood. The poet was in a sad, regretful mood when a crow shook down the dust (fine snow) from a hemlock tree onto him. This simple, unexpected touch of nature lifted his spirits and saved a part of his day that he had thought wasted. The crow and hemlock (usually symbols of gloom/poison) are used positively here. Themes: nature's healing power, transformation of mood, and finding joy and hope in small, ordinary moments. Poetic devices: symbolism, imagery.

subject: English
text: Fire and Ice by Robert Frost reflects on how the world might end. 'Fire' symbolises desire, greed, lust and passion; 'Ice' symbolises hatred, coldness, indifference and rigidity. The poet says some believe the world will end in fire, others in ice. From his experience of desire, he sides with those who favour fire; but he adds that ice (hatred) is also great and would suffice to destroy. The poem warns that uncontrolled human emotions — both intense desire and cold hatred — are destructive. Themes: destructive human emotions, self-restraint. Devices: symbolism, brevity, alliteration.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight (Poems): A Tiger in the Zoo
text: A Tiger in the Zoo by Leslie Norris contrasts a caged tiger with a free one. In the zoo, the mighty tiger stalls in a small cage, quiet in 'his quiet rage', ignoring visitors and staring at the stars at night — helpless and imprisoned. The poet imagines the tiger in the wild: lurking in shadows, sliding through long grass, hunting deer, and terrorising villagers near the water hole — powerful and free. The poem criticises the caging of wild animals. Themes: loss of freedom, cruelty of captivity, and man's disruption of nature. Devices: contrast, imagery, metaphor.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight (Poems): How to Tell Wild Animals
text: How to Tell Wild Animals by Carolyn Wells is a humorous poem that comically 'teaches' how to identify dangerous wild animals — but in each case the method of identification is fatal or absurd. For example, if a large tawny beast roars at you as you die, it is an Asian Lion; if a striped creature eats you, it is a Bengal Tiger; a leopard leaps on you repeatedly; a bear hugs you hard; a crocodile weeps ('crocodile tears'); a hyena smiles. The humour lies in identifying animals by how they attack. Themes: humour and satire through irony and exaggeration. Devices: hyperbole, humour, rhyme.

subject: English
text: The Ball Poem by John Berryman deals with loss and growing up. A young boy loses his ball, which bounces into the water and is gone. The poet does not offer money for a new ball, because the point is not the ball's price but the boy's first experience of loss and the sense of responsibility. Through this, the boy learns 'the epistemology of loss' — how to accept losing things in life, since everyone must one day face loss. Themes: the inevitability of loss, growing up, and learning to cope with grief. Devices: symbolism (ball = things we cherish/lose), imagery.

subject: English
text: Amanda! by Robin Klein presents the tension between a child's freedom and adult control. Amanda is constantly nagged by an adult (parent): don't bite nails, sit straight, do homework, clean shoes, etc. In response, Amanda escapes into her imagination — she dreams of being a mermaid drifting in a green sea, an orphan roaming the streets freely, and Rapunzel in a tower who would never let her hair down. The poem shows a child suffocated by constant instructions. Themes: the loss of a child's freedom, over-restriction by adults, and the power of imagination as escape. Devices: imagery, contrast, allusion (Rapunzel).

subject: English
text: The Trees by Adrienne Rich uses trees as an extended metaphor. The trees inside a house are moving out to the forest where they belong — all night they struggle to free their roots and leaves from the confines of the house/glass. By morning they will stand in the forest. The poem can be read literally (nature reclaiming its place) and symbolically (women or oppressed people breaking free from confinement to reclaim freedom and identity). Themes: freedom versus captivity, nature reclaiming itself, and liberation. Devices: personification, metaphor, imagery.

subject: English
text: Fog by Carl Sandburg is a very short poem that describes fog using a single extended metaphor: the fog comes 'on little cat feet'. It sits silently overlooking the harbour and city, like a cat sitting on its haunches, and then moves on. The comparison of fog to a cat captures how it arrives quietly, settles, and leaves without notice. Themes: the beauty and quiet movement of nature, observed through a simple, vivid image. Devices: metaphor (fog = cat), imagery, personification. It is an example of imagist poetry — conveying a picture in few words.

subject: English
chapter: First Flight (Poems): The Tale of Custard the Dragon
text: The Tale of Custard the Dragon by Ogden Nash is a humorous ballad. Belinda lives with her pets: a kitten (Ink), a mouse (Blink), a little yellow dog (Mustard), and a cowardly dragon named Custard, who is always crying for a safe cage. The others mock Custard for being a coward while boasting of their own bravery. But when a fearsome pirate breaks in, all the 'brave' ones flee or hide, and it is the 'cowardly' Custard who fights and gobbles up the pirate. Afterwards, they resume teasing him. Themes: appearances can be deceptive, real courage shows in action, and gentle satire on boastfulness. Devices: humour, imagery, rhyme.

subject: English
text: For Anne Gregory by William Butler Yeats is a conversation about love and inner versus outer beauty. A young man is attracted to Anne Gregory's beautiful yellow (honey-coloured) hair. The poet tells her that men love her for her external beauty (her hair), not for herself alone. Anne says she could dye her hair a different colour so that young men would love her for herself. The poet replies that only God can love her 'for herself alone and not her yellow hair'. Themes: the difference between physical beauty and true/inner worth, and the nature of human versus divine love. Devices: symbolism, dialogue.

subject: English
chapter: Footprints Without Feet: A Triumph of Surgery
text: A Triumph of Surgery by James Herriot. Tricki, a small dog owned by the rich and doting Mrs Pumphrey, has become greatly overfed and ill (fat, listless) due to too many treats. The vet Mr Herriot takes Tricki to his surgery, where he simply gives him a proper diet and exercise (no rich food, only water and normal feeding) alongside other dogs. Tricki quickly recovers and becomes healthy and lively. Mrs Pumphrey believes it is a 'triumph of surgery', though no surgery was done. Themes: harmful over-pampering of pets, the importance of discipline and moderation, and gentle humour/satire on the wealthy.

subject: English
chapter: Footprints Without Feet: The Thief's Story
text: The Thief's Story by Ruskin Bond. Hari Singh, a fifteen-year-old thief, befriends Anil, a kind and carefree young writer, by offering to work for him in exchange for being taught to read and write. Anil trusts him, feeds him and pays him. One night Hari steals Anil's money and runs to the station, but at the last moment he cannot board the train — the thought of losing Anil's trust, friendship and the chance to become educated stops him. He returns and quietly puts the money back. Anil, who seems to know, still trusts him and offers to teach him. Themes: the transforming power of trust, kindness and education; redemption and the value of relationships over money.

subject: English
chapter: Footprints Without Feet: The Midnight Visitor
text: The Midnight Visitor by Robert Arthur. Ausable, an unglamorous, overweight secret agent, is not the typical dashing spy. In his hotel room, his rival Max appears with a gun to steal a secret report. Ausable stays calm and invents a story about a balcony outside the window (which does not exist) and claims the police keep entering through it. When a knock comes at the door (actually a waiter Ausable had ordered), Max panics, believes the police are coming, and climbs out of the window onto the non-existent balcony — and falls. Themes: intelligence and presence of mind triumph over force; appearances are deceptive. Devices: irony, suspense.

subject: English
chapter: Footprints Without Feet: A Question of Trust
text: A Question of Trust by Victor Canning. Horace Danby is a respectable, successful lock-maker who is secretly a thief; every year he robs a safe to buy rare books. While robbing a house, he is caught by an attractive young woman who claims to be the owner's wife. She persuades him to open the safe for her, saying she has forgotten the combination and needs her jewels, promising not to report him. Trusting her, Horace opens the safe (leaving his fingerprints, having removed his gloves). Later he learns she was actually another thief who tricked him; he is arrested for the robbery she committed. Themes: irony, misplaced trust, and the deceiver deceived. Devices: situational irony.

subject: English
chapter: Footprints Without Feet: Footprints Without Feet
text: Footprints Without Feet by H.G. Wells is science fiction. Griffin, a brilliant but lawless scientist, discovers how to make his body invisible by changing its refractive index. Becoming invisible, he misuses his power — he sets fire to his landlord's house, wanders the cold streets of London, and takes refuge in a big London store, then steals clothes and money. In the village of Iping, his mysterious behaviour and bandaged appearance arouse suspicion; when discovered, he uses invisibility to escape and commits robbery, leaving only footprints. Themes: misuse of scientific knowledge, the dangers of power without morality, and lawlessness. Devices: science fiction, irony.

subject: English
chapter: Footprints Without Feet: The Making of a Scientist
text: The Making of a Scientist by Robert W. Peterson is about Richard Ebright, who grew into a top scientist. As a child in Pennsylvania he collected butterflies and had a curious, driven mind. His mother encouraged his learning. Losing interest in mere collecting, he began real science projects — studying the cause of a viral disease in monarch butterflies, the purpose of gold spots on a monarch pupa, and eventually a theory on how cells read their DNA. He won science fairs (including Westinghouse). Key qualities: curiosity, a first-rate mind, competitive spirit and hard work. Themes: what makes a scientist — curiosity, determination, good guidance, and the will to win for the right reasons.

subject: English
text: The Necklace by Guy de Maupassant. Matilda Loisel, a pretty but discontented woman, longs for a rich, elegant life beyond her modest means. Invited to a grand ball, she borrows a diamond necklace from her wealthy friend Madame Forestier to look glamorous. She loses the necklace at the ball. Too proud to confess, she and her husband borrow a huge sum to buy a replacement and spend ten hard years of poverty repaying the debt, losing her youth and beauty. Later, Madame Forestier reveals the borrowed necklace was fake, worth almost nothing. Themes: the destructiveness of vanity and greed, the value of honesty, and the irony of fate. Devices: dramatic/situational irony.

subject: English
text: Bholi by K.A. Abbas. Sulekha, nicknamed 'Bholi' (simpleton), is a neglected girl — she had smallpox marks, stammered, and was considered dull. Sent to school (only because her father wanted to please an official), she gains confidence and education under a kind teacher. Years later, at her arranged wedding, the greedy old bridegroom Bishamber demands a dowry of five thousand rupees. The now-educated and self-respecting Bholi boldly rejects the marriage, refusing to marry a greedy man who insults her. She chooses to serve her parents and teach at her school. Themes: the transforming power of education, women's empowerment and self-respect, and evils of dowry and neglect of daughters.

subject: English
chapter: Footprints Without Feet: The Book that Saved the Earth
text: The Book that Saved the Earth by Claire Boiko is a humorous science-fiction play set in the future, looking back at the (imagined) Martian invasion of 2040. The Martians, led by the boastful Think-Tank and his assistant Noodle, plan to invade Earth. Their probe Omega lands in a library and finds a book of nursery rhymes (Mother Goose). Think-Tank hilariously misinterprets the rhymes — believing 'Humpty Dumpty' shows Martians being overthrown and that Earthlings are dangerous giants. Terrified by his own misreading, he calls off the invasion and flees. Thus a book of nursery rhymes 'saves the Earth'. Themes: the power of books/knowledge, humour and satire on arrogance and ignorance.

subject: English
text: Determiners are words placed before nouns to specify quantity, definiteness, or possession. Types: articles (a, an, the), demonstratives (this, that, these, those), possessives (my, your, his), quantifiers (some, any, much, many, few, little, a lot of), numbers, and distributives (each, every, either, neither). Use 'a' before consonant sounds, 'an' before vowel sounds, 'the' for specific/known things. 'Few/little' = hardly any (negative); 'a few/a little' = some (positive). Subject-Verb Concord (agreement): the verb must agree with its subject in number and person. Singular subject takes a singular verb ('He plays'), plural takes plural ('They play'). Collective nouns usually take a singular verb; 'each/every/either/neither' take singular verbs; two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb.

subject: English
text: Tenses show the time of an action. Present: simple (plays), continuous (is playing), perfect (has played), perfect continuous (has been playing). Past: simple (played), continuous (was playing), perfect (had played), perfect continuous (had been playing). Future: simple (will play), continuous (will be playing), perfect (will have played). Use the correct tense as per the time and context; gap-filling questions test this. Modals are helping verbs showing mood/attitude: can/could (ability, permission), may/might (possibility, permission), must (obligation, certainty), shall/should (advice, duty), will/would (willingness, future, polite requests), ought to (moral duty), need/dare. Modals are followed by the base form of the verb (e.g. 'She can sing').

subject: English
text: Reported (indirect) speech tells what someone said without quoting exactly (no inverted commas). Changes from direct speech: the reporting verb, tense (present shifts to past: 'is' to 'was', 'play' to 'played'), pronouns, and time/place words (now to then, today to that day, here to there). (1) Statements: use 'that' — He said, 'I am busy' becomes He said that he was busy. (2) Questions: use 'asked' with 'if/whether' (for yes/no) or the question word; change to statement order, no question mark — She said, 'Where are you going?' becomes She asked where I was going. (3) Commands and requests: use 'told/ordered/requested' + 'to' + verb — He said, 'Open the door' becomes He told me to open the door; 'Please help me' becomes He requested me to help him. Negative commands use 'not to'.

subject: English
text: A formal letter (100-120 words) follows a fixed format: (1) Sender's address, (2) Date, (3) Receiver's designation and address, (4) Subject line (brief purpose), (5) Salutation (Sir/Madam), (6) Body in clear paragraphs — introduction (purpose), details, and a closing request, (7) Complimentary close ('Yours faithfully' when name unknown, 'Yours sincerely' when known), (8) Sender's name and signature. Types tested: letters to the editor (public issues), letters of complaint (state the problem, order/bill details, inconvenience, and expected action), letters of enquiry, and applications/placing orders. Keep the tone formal, polite, clear and to the point. Marks are awarded for format, content, and expression/accuracy.

subject: English
text: An analytical paragraph (100-120 words) is written on a given map, chart, graph, table, cue or outline, describing and interpreting the information. Structure: (1) Introduction — state what the visual/data is about. (2) Body — describe the main features, compare figures, note trends (increase/decrease, highest/lowest), and give supporting details in a logical order. (3) Conclusion — a brief overall interpretation or summary of what the data shows. Write in one or two coherent paragraphs, in a formal, objective tone (no personal opinion or 'I think'). Use appropriate connectors (however, whereas, in contrast, overall) and the correct tense. Marks are for content (accurate reading of data), organisation, and language accuracy.
